Corpus › Other › class

class

Translation status: English reader-locale proof. Term names and code fences follow the en pack; supporting prose may still be English.

Declares a concrete type with fields and methods.

Aliases: class, struct

Syntax: class <name> [<type-params>] <block>

Category#

class

Related#

  • interface
  • implements

Examples#

radix/corpus/genus/genus.fab (canonical · keyword)#

Declares a concrete type with fields and methods.

# =============================================================================
# class — Declares a concrete type with fields and methods
# =============================================================================
#
# What this teaches:
#   • Declares a concrete type with fields and methods.
#   • Related keywords: interface, implements
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • Using retired bare object literals (`{ key = expr }`) — use `GenusName { field = expr }` instead; bare `{ }` is now a JSON value literal.
#
# See also: interface, implements
# =============================================================================

# Basic class (record type) with fields
#
# class <Name> {
#     <type> <property>
#     <type> <property> = <default>
# }
#
# GRAMMAR:
#   genusDecl :← 'class' ident '{' fieldDecl* '}'
#   instance  :← ident '{' fieldInit (',' fieldInit)* '}'
#
# EXPECTED OUTPUT:
#   Field values for Punctum and Persona instances (defaults and overrides).

class Punctum {
    mut int x
    mut int y
}

class Persona {
    mut string nomen
    # default when omitted at instantiation
    mut int aetas = 0
    mut bool activus = true
}

main {
    # Instantiate with all required fields
    let Punctum p ← Punctum { x = 10, y = 20 }
    print p.x
    print p.y

    # Instantiate with required + optional defaults
    let Persona marcus ← Persona { nomen = "Marcus" }
    print marcus.nomen
    # 0 from default
    print marcus.aetas
    # true from default
    print marcus.activus

    # Override defaults explicitly
    let Persona julia ← Persona { nomen = "Julia", aetas = 25, activus = false }
    print julia.nomen
    print julia.aetas
    print julia.activus
}

Expected output:

10
20
Marcus
0
true
Julia
25
false

radix/corpus/genus/fixum-field-assign-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

A let class field is set only in a construction literal.

class Punctum {
    let int x
    mut int y
}

main {
    mut Punctum p ← Punctum { x = 1, y = 2 }
    p.x ← 5
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/genus/initializer-type-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

A field initializer whose type does not match the declared field is a check error.

# =============================================================================
# class — a field initializer has the wrong type for the declared field
# =============================================================================
# Each field initializer in a construction literal must match the type the
# class declares for that field. A `text` initializer for an `int` field is a
# check error, so a mismatched value never enters a class.

class A { mut int x }

main {
    let A a ← A { x = "text" }
    print a.x
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/genus/missing-field-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

Omitting a required field from a construction literal without a source is a check error.

# =============================================================================
# class — a construction literal without a source omits a required field
# =============================================================================
# A construction literal builds a complete value. Without a `from` source to
# copy from, every declared field must be named; leaving one out is a check
# error, so a class value never exists half-built.

class A {
    mut int x
    mut int y
}

main {
    let A a ← A { x = 1 }
    print a.x
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.

radix/corpus/genus/unknown-field-reject.fab (supporting · reject)#

A construction literal naming a field the class does not declare is a check error.

# =============================================================================
# class — a construction literal names a field the class does not declare
# =============================================================================
# Every key in a construction literal must be a declared field. A key that the
# class does not declare — a typo, or a field from another type — is a check
# error, so the value can never diverge from the declaration.

class A { mut int x }

main {
    let A a ← A { x = 1, z = 2 }
    print a.x
}

Expected: compilation rejects this example.
